Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas · Conversation, family & daily routines

talk verb and noun

also speak, chat, converse, have a talk, conversation, have a chat with, engage in conversation, shoot the breeze, sling the bull, give a talk, small talk, talk something over, have a talk with

classical

Cic. Att. 8.14.2: ego tēcum tamquam mēcum loquor
Ter. Eun. 86: Quis hīc loquitur?
Traupman 383

loquor, loquī, locūtus sum

verb, third conjugation, deponent

talk, speak

Lewis & Short: “in the language of common life, in the tone of conversation”. With cum and the ablative, talk to or with someone; with dē, talk about. To speak in public, as an orator, is dīcere.

Other words

  • sermō, sermōnis m. — a talk, conversation

    noun, third declension · classical · Cic. Att. 5.1.3: in prīmīs nōbīs sermō isque multus dē tē fuit; Cic. Off. 1.136: quibuscum sermōnem cōnferēmus; Traupman 296; Traupman 390

    Sermōnem cum aliquō cōnferre or habēre, to have a talk with someone; also a language (see language).

  • colloquor, colloquī, collocūtus sum — talk together, converse

    verb, third conjugation, deponent · also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 1.32: quod conloquimur inter nōs; Cic. Q. fr. 2.8.1: et obloquāre et colloquāre

    With cum aliquō or inter sē; the noun is colloquium.

  • fābulor, fābulārī, fābulātus sum — chat, talk

    verb, first conjugation, deponent · also used · classical · Ter. Ph. 654: ut apertē tibi nunc fābuler; Plaut. Epid. 237: fābulārī inter sēsē; Traupman 289

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; posteā Suet., Gell.)

    Lewis & Short: “esp. freq. in Plaut.; not in Cic.”.

  • for, fārī, fātus sum — speak; of a child, begin to talk

    verb, first conjugation, deponent, defective · also used · classical · Varr. LL 6.52: puerī dīcuntur īnfantēs; cum id faciunt, jam fārī; Suet. Aug. 94.7: cum prīmum fārī coepisset

    (vōx plērumque poētica: Verg., Hor.; dē puerīs prīmum loquentibus Varr., Gell., Suet.)

    Hence īnfāns, “not (yet) speaking”.

  • cōnfābulor, cōnfābulārī, cōnfābulātus sum — have a chat, talk together

    verb, first conjugation, deponent · also used · classical · Plaut. Merc. 1.2.76; Ter. Hec. 1.2.107 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 95; Traupman 289

    (vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut., Ter.)

    Lewis & Short: early and colloquial for colloquor; with cum aliquō.

  • sermōnēs cōnferre (cum aliquō) — engage in conversation

    also used · classical · Plaut. Poen. prol. 34: dum sermōnēs fābulandī cōnferant (Lewis & Short s.v. sermō); Traupman 96; Traupman 296

  • sermunculus, sermunculī m. — small talk, gossip, tittle-tattle

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Deiot. 33: urbānī sermunculī (Lewis & Short); Traupman 390

    Lewis & Short: common talk, rumour; rare but classical.

Examples

  • ego tēcum tamquam mēcum loquor

    Talking to you is like talking to myself.Cic. Att. 8.14.2

  • Hōc enim ūnō praestāmus vel maximē ferīs, quod conloquimur inter nōs

    For in this one thing above all we surpass the beasts: that we talk with one anotherCic. de Or. 1.32

  • ībat rēx obsitus aevō et comitem Aenēān juxtā nātumque tenēbat ingrediēns variōque viam sermōne levābat

    The old king walked along, keeping Aeneas and his son beside him, and lightened the road with talk of this and that.Verg. A. 8.307–309

  • fīlius Croesī rēgis, cum jam fārī per aetātem posset, īnfāns erat

    King Croesus’s son, when he was old enough to talk, still could not speakGell. 5.9.1

  • sermō puerīlis (stultus, quotīdiānus)

    childish (silly, everyday) talkTraupman 390

  • sermōnem habēre

    to give a talkTraupman 390

  • cum aliquō dīligenter colloquī

    to have a talk with someoneTraupman 390

  • aliquid cum aliquō commūnicāre

    to talk something over with someoneTraupman 390

See also speak, chatter, stop talking, speak up, talk on the phone, say, in a low voice.
